analysis.one_liner: Lets adults buy hearing aids over the counter for mild-to-moderate hearing loss without a prescription.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 115th Congress, but Congress enacted its core language that same year in the FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FDA to create a new category of over-the-counter hearing aids for adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss, sold in stores, by mail, or online without a prescription or a licensed professional's involvement. It set deadlines for safety rules, output limits, and clear labeling, and it barred states from adding their own prescription requirements. Today, hearing aids can cost thousands of dollars per ear, sold mainly through a prescription-and-fitting channel, so the bill aimed to open a cheaper, self-service market.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss, who otherwise face devices costing thousands of dollars per ear sold through mandatory in-person fittings and generally not covered by insurance or Medicare.

how_it_helps.text: The FDA must establish a category of over-the-counter hearing aids that can be sold to adults without a prescription or any licensed professional's involvement, through in-person transactions, by mail, or online.
The regulations must provide reasonable assurances of safety and efficacy, set output limits, and require labeling that tells consumers how to report problems and when to see a physician.
The bill set a clock: proposed regulations within 3 years of enactment and final rules within 180 days after the public comment period closed.

States and localities could not impose their own hearing-product rules that restrict or interfere with the sale of over-the-counter devices, including any requirement for a prescription or a licensed professional's sign-off.
The FDA also had to finalize existing guidance clarifying which hearing products are medical devices and which are simpler personal sound amplifiers, so consumers know what they are buying.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed hearing aid dispensers and audiologists who earn revenue from mandatory in-person fittings and prescription sales, and manufacturers whose high-margin business depends on that professional channel.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hearing aid dispensers and fitting clinics

drawbacks.text: Bypassing a professional exam means some users may not learn whether their hearing loss has a treatable medical cause; the bill addresses this only through labeling that advises consumers to consult a physician promptly.
The devices are limited to adults over 18 with mild-to-moderate loss, so children and people with severe hearing loss still have to go through the professional channel.
The bill preempts state rules for hearing products, overriding any stricter state-level consumer protections with the federal standard.
The safety standard is 'reasonable assurances of safety and efficacy' rather than full clinical-trial review, a lighter bar that supporters of professional fitting said was too permissive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and concrete: a regulated, cheaper path to hearing devices for a common condition that insurance rarely covers, with federal output limits and labeling to manage the safety risk. The strongest honest objection is that some buyers will skip a medical evaluation they need, and the bill's answer — a label — is imperfect. The main real cost falls on dispensers' revenue, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on March 21, 2017 with Republican Charles Grassley and Democrats Maggie Hassan and Johnny Isakson listed as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no markup, no hearing, no vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral.
The bill's language would have required the FDA to set final rules on a fixed timeline and preempt state prescription requirements for over-the-counter hearing aids.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The policy did not die with the bill: Congress folded the same over-the-counter hearing aid provisions into the FDA Reauthorization Act of 2017, which became law, so consumers ultimately got the cheaper self-service option. Hearing aid dispensers and audiologists still lost the prescription-and-fitting gatekeeping requirement, but they avoided a standalone fight over this specific bill, and manufacturers gained a new direct-to-consumer market either way.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from day one: a Democrat (Warren) and a senior Republican (Grassley) led it, and the five later cosponsors split 3 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill creates a new over-the-counter category that lets manufacturers sell directly to consumers in stores and online, while still subjecting those devices to federal safety rules and output limits. Consumers get cheaper devices; manufacturers get a bigger market.

industries.industry: Audiologists and licensed hearing aid dispensers
industries.note: The bill removes the requirement that a licensed professional prescribe, fit, or otherwise intervene before a consumer can buy a hearing aid, and bars states from re-imposing it. Those mandatory fittings and prescription sales are where this profession's hearing aid revenue comes from, and the public's savings come largely out of that margin.

Opening over-the-counter sales through in-person, mail, and online channels creates a new product line for drugstores, electronics retailers, and e-commerce sellers. That competition is what pushes prices down for buyers.
